---
title: "Data & references"
---

Every map on this site is built from public, open-source data. This page describes what
those datasets are, where they come from, and how they are licensed, and then lists
the literature the analysis and narrative rest on. The full version
— version strings, file paths, record counts, access dates, and known issues — is
in [`docs/data-sources.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/data-sources.md).

Two principles govern the data on this project. First, **Phase 1 uses open data
only** — no partner or restricted data is used or published. Second, **no precise
puma location is ever published** (see the note at the foot of this page).

## The data

### Where animals were recorded

- **GBIF** (Global Biodiversity Information Facility) — the main occurrence source,
  pulled as a citable, DOI-stamped download, so the exact
  record set is reproducible. Records carry a coordinate-uncertainty value that the
  analysis respects when snapping points to units.
- **iNaturalist** — community wildlife observations.
  iNaturalist obscures many sensitive species by default, but **not** mountain lions
  in California, which is exactly why the sensitive-data handling on this project is strict.
- **GBIF target-group background** — for the bobcat occupancy model, a second, much
  larger GBIF pull of *all* vertebrate records across the region stands in for
  "where did people look at all," which is what lets the model separate effort from
  presence.

### Where habitat is protected

- **CPAD** (California Protected Areas Database) — parks, preserves, watershed lands
  and other fee-owned open space, with the unit hierarchy the occupancy site
  definition needs.
- **CCED** (California Conservation Easement Database) — conservation easements on
  otherwise private land, held as a separate layer and combined with CPAD for total
  protected coverage.
- **TIGER/Line county boundaries** (US Census, via `tigris`) — the ten-county study
  frame.

### What the landscape is made of?

- **ESA WorldCover 2021** — 10 m land cover (trees, shrub, built-up, cropland, and
  so on), the base habitat layer. A known trade-off: WorldCover
  under-maps California chaparral badly compared with older US products, which is why
  urban-intensity comes from human modification instead.
- **Global Human Modification (gHM) v3, 2022** (Theobald et al. 2024) — a 0–1 index
  of how heavily each area is modified by people; the dominant term in the puma
  resistance surface.
- **SILVIS housing density** — block-level housing as a second human-footprint
  source.
- **AWS Terrain Tiles** (via `elevatr`) — elevation, from which slope is derived.
  The tiles blend several public elevation sources at roughly 30 m effective
  resolution here.

### Roads and traffic

- **OpenStreetMap roads** (Geofabrik NorCal extract) — the road network, classified
  by type. Because roads are a barrier only when busy, road presence alone is not
  enough.
- **Caltrans AADT** — annual average daily traffic counts, which turn "a road is
  here" into "how much traffic crosses here." A structural caveat: traffic count stations cluster on busy roads, so any spatial fill of the
  gaps has a built-in upward bias, handled with a source flag.

### Road mortality (pending)

- **CROS** (California Roadkill Observation System) / **UC Davis Road Ecology
  Center** — the intended wildlife–vehicle collision source. Record-level access is
  still pending, so the collision-risk question is currently answered as a
  risk-overlap proxy, not as a mortality point layer.

### Population context

There is **no** repeated regional census of Bay Area pumas or bobcats — nothing like
the national tiger census that anchors the sister project. A single statewide puma
abundance estimate exists (the California Mountain Lion Project, roughly 3,200–4,500
statewide) and is cited only as one-time context. **No statewide
bobcat abundance estimate exists at all**.

## Licences

Every dataset is used within its licence, with attribution where required. 
[`docs/data-sources.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/data-sources.md) §7,
holds the full terms.

| Dataset | Licence | Attribution | Redistribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPAD / CCED | Open (CC-BY; "no restrictions on public use") | Yes | Allowed |
| GBIF | CC0 / CC-BY (varies per record) | Yes | Check per record |
| iNaturalist | CC-BY / CC-BY-NC (varies per observer) | Yes | Check per record |
| CROS | Confirm terms (pending) | Yes | Confirm |
| AWS Terrain / TIGER | Public domain | No | Allowed |
| ESA WorldCover | CC-BY 4.0 | Yes | Allowed |
| gHM v3 (Theobald 2024) | CC-BY 4.0 | Yes | Allowed |
| SILVIS housing | USDA FS / SILVIS (acknowledgement requested) | Yes | Allowed |
| OpenStreetMap | ODbL | Yes | Share-alike |
| Caltrans AADT | California public data | Yes | Informational |

Dataset citations (the datasets themselves, with DOIs and access dates) are in
`docs/data-sources.md`. The literature the analysis and narrative reference is below.

## References

The list is grouped by role. It is author–date; a `.bib` conversion is planned if
the site moves to Quarto citation handling.

### Population and status

- Dellinger, J.A., Gustafson, K.D., Gammons, D.J., Ernest, H.B., & Torres, S.G.
  (2020). Minimum habitat thresholds required for conserving mountain lion genetic
  diversity. *Ecology and Evolution*, 10(19), 10687–10696. — method paper behind the
  statewide abundance estimate.
- Dellinger, J.A., et al. (2019). Using mountain lion habitat selection in
  management. *The Journal of Wildlife Management*, 84(2). DOI: 10.1002/jwmg.21798.
- California Department of Fish and Wildlife (2025). *Status Review of the Petitioned
  Southern California / Central Coast ESU of Mountain Lion in California.* December
  2025 (CDFW document portal, DocumentID 239679 / 239696) — the review the Fish and
  Game Commission relied on.
- California Fish and Game Commission (2026). Vote to list the Southern California /
  Central Coast Distinct Population Segment of mountain lion (*Puma concolor*) as
  **threatened** under CESA, February 12, 2026. Cite the date of the vote; the formal
  findings and regulatory effective date follow at a later meeting.

::: {.callout-note title="On the puma listing"}
The Santa Cruz Mountains population — the one anchoring this project's connectivity
story — falls within the listed DPS. The listing is recent and post-dates the
project's model training; it was verified against the primary Commission notice.
Because the formal effective date follows the vote, this site cites the **February
12, 2026 vote**, not an effective date, and points to the primary Commission notice
for the adopted findings.
:::

### Bay Area felid research

- Hansen, K.W., Morgan, J.J., De Alfaro, L., Wilmers, C.C., & Ocampo-Peñuela, N.
  (2025). *Variation in anthropogenic tolerance alters dispersal capacity of a large
  carnivore.* bioRxiv 2025.09.29.677867 (preprint). Step-selection models for 84
  GPS-collared Santa Cruz Mountains pumas (2009–2024). **The local calibration source
  for the puma resistance surface** — covariate choice, effect directions, and the
  log-inverse traffic transform. Data/code: Dryad 10.5061/dryad.44j0zpctn.
- Wilmers, C.C., Wang, Y., Nickel, B., et al. (2013). Scale-dependent behavioral
  responses to human development by a large predator, the puma. *PLoS ONE*, 8(4),
  e60590. — housing-density-as-covariate precedent for Santa Cruz pumas.
- Nisi, A.C., Benson, J.F., King, R., & Wilmers, C.C. (2023). Habitat fragmentation
  reduces survival and drives source–sink dynamics for a large carnivore. *Ecological
  Applications*, 33(4), e2822. — basis for weighting roads and traffic as a barrier.
- Felidae Conservation Fund / Bay Area Puma Project publications — relevant to the
  deferred partner data and the coexistence framing.

### Road ecology

- UC Davis Road Ecology Center (Shilling et al.) — annual California
  wildlife–vehicle collision hotspot reports; the published-hotspot fallback if
  record-level CROS access is not granted.
- Comparative analysis of puma road-crossing locations versus roadkill hotspots for
  siting crossings and fencing.

### Corridor corroboration (grey literature)

- Bay Area Critical Linkages / Conservation Lands Network — Santa Cruz Mountains and
  Coyote Valley linkage assessments. Open Space Authority of Santa Clara Valley,
  *Coyote Valley Landscape Linkage*; Santa Cruz Mountains Linkage *Conceptual Area
  Protection Plan*. Cited as field corroboration of the modelled corridor, not as
  method.

## Sensitive data

::: {.callout-important title="No precise puma locations are published"}
iNaturalist does not obscure mountain lions in California, so this project holds
precise puma records that could expose real animals if published as points.
Published puma outputs are therefore always generalised — continuous surfaces at a
1 km grain, or summaries at the open-space-unit level — never point maps, camera
locations, den sites, or kill sites. Bobcat data, lower-sensitivity, is published at
finer resolution but reviewed under the same process. The full policy is in
[`docs/sensitive-data-policy.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/sensitive-data-policy.md).
:::

The complete data provenance, including every version, access date, DOI, and known
issues, is in
[`docs/data-sources.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/data-sources.md);
the full literature bibliography is in
[`docs/references.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/references.md).
